question: Do home remedies for colds work?

say: Every winter, you spend a small fortune on vitamin C tablets, catch a cold anyway, and wonder what went wrong.
Your body was built to beat a cold on its own, and most people start to feel better within one to two weeks.
Daily vitamin C didn't stop ordinary people catching colds in trials, and starting it once you're ill made no consistent difference.
So eat the orange and skip the fizzy tablets.
Hot water with lemon and honey can work about as well as cough syrup, but never give honey to a baby under one.
And retire the bowl of hot water under a towel: there's no strong evidence it helps, and every winter it scalds people, especially young children.
See a doctor if you're getting worse, you're short of breath or have chest pain, or a high temperature lasts over three days, a cough over three weeks, or the cold over ten days.
Go sooner with a very high temperature, a long-term condition, a weak immune system, or a child you're worried about.
If you're struggling to breathe, or can't swallow or are drooling, get emergency help.
Let's get you back to factory settings.

nhssore: NHS, Sore throat (reviewed 8 Apr 2024): "gargle with warm, salty water (children should not try this)"; call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, drooling (a sign of not being able to swallow) or a high-pitched sound as you breathe
nhscold: NHS, Common cold (reviewed 22 Mar 2024): "You should begin to feel better in about 1 to 2 weeks"; get plenty of rest, drink lots of fluid; "There's little evidence that supplements such as vitamin C, echinacea or garlic prevent colds or help you get better more quickly"; see a GP if: a high temperature for more than 3 days; symptoms get worse; temperature very high, or hot, cold or shivery; short of breath or chest pain; worried about your child's symptoms; not better after 10 days; a cough for more than 3 weeks; a long-term medical condition; a weakened immune system
bba2025: NHS and British Burn Association joint warning, 18 Nov 2025 (Royal Devon NHS news): urging the public to avoid steam inhalation for coughs and colds; "Each winter, NHS hospitals treat patients - especially young children - who have sustained serious scalds and burns"; "There is no strong scientific evidence that steam inhalation helps relieve colds or blocked noses"
oduwole2018: Oduwole O et al. Honey for acute cough in children. Cochrane 2018 (CD007094): six trials, 899 children aged 12 months to 18 years; honey probably reduces cough more than placebo; little or no difference between honey and dextromethorphan; honey not advised under 12 months
singh2017: Singh M et al. Heated, humidified air for the common cold. Cochrane 2017 (CD001728): 6 trials, 387 people; evidence insufficient to show benefit; minor adverse events in 2 trials
nhscough: NHS, Cough (reviewed 8 Dec 2023): "hot lemon and honey, which can have a similar effect to cough syrup"; "not suitable for babies under 1 year old"; do not give hot drinks to small children
hemila2013: Hemilä H, Chalker E. Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold. Cochrane 2013: regular supplements in the general population, catching a cold RR 0.97 (0.94 to 1.00), 29 comparisons, 11,306 people; taken after a cold starts, "No consistent effect"; "routine vitamin C supplementation is not justified"
